html:
The Wright Flyer was the first powered, heavier-than-air machine to make a sustained and controlled flight with a pilot aboard. The Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, flew it on 17 December 1903 near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

The brothers ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. Others had built gliders and engines, but the Wrights saw that the real problem was control: how a pilot could steer and balance in the air. They solved it with "wing warping", twisting the wingtips to roll the plane, together with a movable front elevator and a rear rudder. They tested ideas with kites, gliders and a homemade wind tunnel, and built their own light petrol engine of about 12 horsepower, driving two propellers.

That December morning Orville flew first, for 12 seconds and about 37 metres. They made four flights that day; the longest, by Wilbur, lasted 59 seconds and covered 260 metres. Then a gust of wind wrecked the plane. Few people noticed at first. Only in 1908, with public flights in France and the US, was the world convinced.

From there flight moved fast. Within eleven years aircraft were fighting in the First World War, and passenger airlines followed in the 1920s. Within 66 years people stood on the Moon (see first Moon landing); Neil Armstrong carried a piece of the Flyer's wing fabric with him. The original plane hangs in the Smithsonian in Washington.
